versions.name: King James Version
versions.notes: Authorized in 1611 for the Church of England, the King James Version is the most historically influential English Bible. Its 1769 revision standardized spelling and punctuation and remains the familiar 'King James' text — stately, formal, and rhythmically memorable.

versions.name: American Standard Version
versions.notes: The 1901 American answer to the English Revised Version, this formal translation followed the older manuscripts then known and modernized Elizabethan grammar. Its faithful, literal style made it a trusted study text that later revisions would build on.

versions.name: World English Bible
versions.notes: A modern English translation produced specifically to be free of copyright, so it can be copied and redistributed without restriction. Built on the American Standard Version and updated into contemporary idiom, it keeps a literal feel while reading clearly.

versions.name: Webster Bible
versions.notes: Noah Webster's 1833 revision smoothed the King James Bible's archaic language — replacing 'thy' and 'ye' with plain modern words — while keeping the KJV’s wording and cadence largely intact.

versions.name: Young's Literal Translation
versions.notes: Robert Young's translation aims for maximum literalness, rendering the original word order and tenses as closely as English allows. Its distinctive, sometimes stilted feel is prized by readers who want to see the shape of the Greek and Hebrew underneath.

versions.name: Darby Translation
versions.notes: The English New Testament and Bible of John Nelson Darby, a Brethren teacher and scholar. Known for its literal approach and its reliance on the Received Text, it is valued by students of the original wording.

versions.name: Bible in Basic English
versions.notes: A translation into a vocabulary of roughly 1,000 common English words, created for new speakers of the language. It trades literary polish for utter simplicity and clarity.

versions.name: Geneva Bible
versions.notes: The Bible of the English Reformation — Shakespeare and the Pilgrims both knew it. Its outspoken marginal notes so alarmed King James that he commissioned the rival translation that bears his name.

versions.name: King James Version with Apocrypha
versions.notes: The King James text with the deuterocanonical books — the Apocrypha — included alongside the Protestant canon, the older, Catholic-leaning arrangement. Here for readers who want those books in the KJV’s words.

versions.name: Douay-Rheims 1899
versions.notes: The classic English Catholic Bible, translated from the Latin Vulgate. The 1899 Bishop Challoner revision smoothed the early style into the familiar form still widely used in Catholic editions.

versions.name: Wycliffe Bible (Modern Spelling)
versions.notes: The first complete English Bible, made from the Latin Vulgate by John Wycliffe's circle in the 1380s–90s, centuries before printing. This edition updates the spelling for modern readers.

versions.name: Tyndale New Testament
versions.notes: William Tyndale’s New Testament, the first English translation made directly from Greek. Phrases he coined — 'the powers that be,' 'the salt of the earth’ — still echo in English and in the King James Bible.

versions.name: Revised Version
versions.notes: The 1881–85 revision of the King James by a committee of British scholars, corrected against the oldest manuscripts then known. It began the revision tradition the American Standard Version continued.

versions.name: JPS Tanakh
versions.notes: The Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation of the Hebrew Bible, long the standard Jewish English Bible. Rendered in the spirit of the King James, it reads the Hebrew closely for Jewish readers.

versions.name: Leeser Tanakh
versions.notes: Isaac Leeser's 1854 rendering of the Hebrew Scriptures, the first major Jewish English Bible produced in America. For decades it was the Jewish community's standard translation of the Tenakh.

versions.name: Noyes Bible
versions.notes: George Rapall Noyes's translation of the Old and New Testaments, valued for its scholarly care and for being among the first English Bibles to draw on the newer critical text of its day.

versions.name: Open English Bible
versions.notes: A modern English Bible released into the public domain, free to use and share in any way. It revises twentieth-century committee work into clean, contemporary English.

versions.name: Majority Standard Bible
versions.notes: A recent formal translation based on the Majority (Byzantine) text of the Greek New Testament. It aims for a consistent, literal rendering a reader can trust for study.

versions.name: Unlocked Literal Bible
versions.notes: An open, literal translation created by the unfoldingWord project, designed to be freely reused for study and as a base for further translation work.

versions.name: Literal Standard Version
versions.notes: A modern English translation that follows the original languages as literally as readable English allows, keeping names and grammatical structures close to the source text.

versions.name: Brenton Septuagint Translation
versions.notes: Lancelot Brenton's English rendering of the Septuagint — the Greek translation of the Old Testament used in the early church. It is a standard way for English readers to meet the Greek Bible.

versions.name: Luther Bible 1912
versions.notes: Martin Luther's translation, the book that helped shape the German language itself. The 1912 revision keeps his vivid, idiomatic German for modern readers.

versions.name: Reina Valera 1909
versions.notes: The classic Spanish Protestant Bible, descended from Casiodoro de Reina's 1569 translation revised by Cipriano de Valera. The 1909 edition is the best-known of that long and beloved line.

versions.name: Louis Segond 1910
versions.notes: Louis Segond's French translation, the standard Protestant Bible in the French-speaking world — clear, dignified, and faithful to the original languages.

versions.name: Clementine Vulgate
versions.notes: Jerome's fourth-century Latin translation, the Vulgate, in the Clementine edition long used by the Catholic Church. This is the Latin Bible itself — the Bible of the Western church for centuries.

versions.name: Westminster Leningrad Codex
versions.notes: The Hebrew Old Testament as preserved in the Leningrad Codex, the oldest complete manuscript of the Hebrew Bible. Reading it is reading the Bible's original language.

versions.name: Septuaginta
versions.notes: The Septuagint — the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament that the New Testament writers themselves quoted. This is the Bible of the early church, in Greek.

versions.name: Textus Receptus
versions.notes: The 'Received Text' — the Greek New Testament compiled by Erasmus and the basis of the King James Version. It lets a reader meet the New Testament as the Reformation translators knew it.

versions.name: Byzantine Greek New Testament
versions.notes: The Greek New Testament in its Byzantine (Majority) textual tradition — the form that dominated the Greek-speaking church for over a thousand years.

versions.name: King James Version (Gutenberg text)
versions.notes: The King James Version again, this time from Project Gutenberg’s digitization of the 1769 text rather than the eBible edition. The wording matches the KJV; only the source file differs.
